reasons: Lake identity gives case_name_full as Samson v. California, court as U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided 2006-06-19, and year 2006.
Lake citations list official 547 U.S. 843, parallels 126 S. Ct. 2193 and 165 L. Ed. 2d 250, and vendor neutral 2006 U.S. LEXIS 4885.

defect.evidence_quote: decide whether a suspicionless search, conducted under the authority of this statute, violates the Constitution. We hold that it does not.
defect.locator_note: content_page.md holding field; text opinion discussion at slip pp. 1, 8, 12 and footnote 5.
defect.problem: The holding is directionally supported but slightly overbroad as phrased. The opinion frames the search as conducted under California's parole-search statute/search condition, with the officer knowing Samson was a parolee, and with California's ban on arbitrary, capricious, or harassing searches in the background.
defect.proposed_fix: Tighten to: A suspicionless search of a known California parolee conducted pursuant to a clearly expressed parole-search condition is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment, so long as it is not arbitrary, capricious, or harassing.

reasons: The opinion supports the core proposition: it concludes the Fourth Amendment does not prohibit a police officer from conducting a suspicionless search of a parolee.
The opinion also ties the analysis to petitioner’s parole status, the plain terms of the parole search condition, and California limits on arbitrary, capricious, or harassing searches.
residual_risks: Short holding may be misread as authorizing any suspicionless parolee search in any jurisdiction or without officer knowledge of parole status.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add the California parole-search condition, known-parolee, and non-arbitrary/non-harassing limits to the one-line holding.

defect.evidence_quote: Nor do we address whether California’s parole search condition is justified as a special need under Griffin v. Wisconsin, 483 U. S. 868 (1987), because our holding under general Fourth Amendment principles renders such an examination unnecessary.
defect.locator_note: content_page.md homes field; opinion slip p. 8 n.3.
defect.problem: The home-role classification as Key — Progeny / Refinement under Special Needs and Administrative Searches is not supported by the disclosed opinion text. The Court expressly declined to decide the special-needs issue and rested on general Fourth Amendment reasonableness.
defect.proposed_fix: Reclassify as an adjacent/boundary parolee-search case, or move it to a parolee/probationer diminished-privacy home rather than treating it as a key special-needs refinement.

reasons: The disclosed opinion says special-needs analysis was unnecessary and not reached.
No lake field independently supports the Special Needs home or the Key — Progeny / Refinement role.
residual_risks: A broader taxonomy might intentionally include non-special-needs boundary cases, but that taxonomy is not disclosed in the evidence.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: If retained on that home page, label it as a boundary/contrast case: suspicionless parolee search upheld under general reasonableness, not special needs.
